prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- Preliminary DNA tests indicate a 3-year-old foster child is the son of a woman being held captive by leftist rebels, Colombian officials announced Friday. Clara Rojas appears in a video released by the kidnappers in July 2002. "There is a very high probability that Juan David belongs to the family of Clara Gonzalez de Rojas," Mario Iguaran Arana, the country's chief federal prosecutor, said at a news conference. The boy, known as "Emmanuel," has been at the center of a hostage drama that raised hopes the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia would liberate some of their hostages. The rebel group, known as FARC for its Spanish acronym, had agreed to release three hostages as part of a deal brokered by Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez. FARC said it would release Emmanuel along with his mother, Clara Rojas, and another woman, Consuelo Gonzalez, but the mission to free the captives fell apart December 31, when the rebel group said it could not release the hostages because of Colombian military operations in the area, according to a FARC statement Chavez read on Venezuelan television. Colombian President Alvaro Uribe denied the group's assertion, saying there were no combat operations in the area near the rebels, and he said the rebels could not release the three hostages because they did not have Emmanuel in custody. He raised the possibility that Emmanuel, who was born in captivity to Rojas, was living in a foster home in the Colombian capital of Bogota. Authorities in Colombia suspect the FARC duped child-welfare authorities by presenting the boy as a child in need of foster care in 2005, he said. On Friday, Iguaran Arana said initial DNA results will be checked against tests being done in European labs to verify the child's identity. There was no immediate response from Venezuela after the announcement concerning Emmanuel's DNA. However, a statement on the Venezuelan government's Web site from earlier Friday said the Colombian government had not allowed Venezuela to participate in the DNA testing. Established in 1964 as the military wing of the Colombian Communist Party, FARC is Colombia's oldest, largest, most capable and best-equipped Marxist rebel group, according to the U.S. Department of State. The United States, the European Union and Colombia classify it as a terrorist group. FARC has justified hostage-taking as a legitimate military tactic in a long-running and complex civil war that also has involved right-wing paramilitary units, government forces and drug traffickers. Fighting has waned, but not stopped, in recent years. Among the group's hostages are three American contractors who were captured when their plane went down in 2003 during a drug-eradication flight, and Ingrid Betancourt, a French-Colombian independent presidential candidate who was kidnapped in 2002. Rojas was kidnapped in 2002 while she managed Betancourt's campaign. Betancourt is perhaps the best-known captive in Colombia, a country plagued by kidnapping.  E-mail to a friend .

BOGOTÁ, Colombia (CNN) — Colombian authorities said Friday that early DNA findings suggest a 3-year-old boy placed in foster care is the child of a woman held hostage by leftist guerrillas.

Clara Rojas was shown in footage issued by her captors in July 2002.

Mario Iguarán Arana, Colombia’s chief federal prosecutor, told reporters there was “a very high probability” that Juan David was related to Clara González de Rojas.

The child, also called “Emmanuel,” became the focus of a hostage-release effort that had generated optimism that the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia might free several captives.

The organization—widely known by its Spanish initials, FARC—had promised to hand over three hostages under an arrangement mediated by Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez. The group said Emmanuel would be freed together with his mother, Clara Rojas, and another female hostage, Consuelo González.

The operation collapsed on December 31. In a statement read by Chávez on Venezuelan television, FARC said Colombian military activity in the region prevented it from releasing the captives.

Colombian President Álvaro Uribe rejected that explanation, insisting there were no combat missions near the rebels. He argued that FARC was unable to produce the three hostages because Emmanuel was no longer in its possession.

Uribe suggested that Emmanuel, whom Rojas gave birth to while in captivity, might instead be living with a foster family in Bogotá, Colombia’s capital. According to him, Colombian officials believe FARC may have deceived child-welfare agencies in 2005 by portraying the boy as a child who required foster care.

Iguarán Arana said Friday that the preliminary DNA findings would be compared with analyses being conducted by European laboratories to confirm the child’s identity.

Venezuela did not immediately respond to the announcement about Emmanuel’s DNA. Earlier Friday, however, a message posted on the Venezuelan government’s website claimed Colombia had prevented Venezuelan representatives from taking part in the genetic testing.

FARC was created in 1964 as the armed branch of the Colombian Communist Party. The U.S. State Department describes it as Colombia’s oldest and largest Marxist insurgent organization, as well as its most capable and best supplied. Colombia, the United States and the European Union have designated the group a terrorist organization.

FARC has defended the seizure of hostages as a lawful wartime strategy within Colombia’s prolonged and complicated civil conflict, which has also included government troops, right-wing paramilitary groups and narcotics traffickers. Although the level of violence has declined in recent years, the fighting has not ended.

The rebels’ captives include three U.S. contractors taken prisoner after their aircraft crashed in 2003 while they were on a drug-eradication mission. FARC also holds Ingrid Betancourt, a dual French-Colombian citizen and independent presidential contender who was abducted in 2002.

Rojas, who managed Betancourt’s political campaign, was kidnapped that same year. In Colombia, where abductions have long been a serious problem, Betancourt is likely the country’s most prominent hostage.

**DNA tests identify boy as son of Colombian hostage Clara Rojas**

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia (CNN)** — DNA tests have confirmed that a young boy living in Colombian foster care is Emmanuel, the son of kidnapped politician Clara Rojas, Colombian authorities said, resolving a mystery that derailed a highly publicized hostage release by FARC rebels.

The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known as FARC, had promised to free Emmanuel along with Rojas and former lawmaker Consuelo González. But the Venezuelan-brokered operation collapsed after Colombian President Álvaro Uribe said the guerrillas could not release the child because he was no longer in their custody.

Investigators then focused on a boy registered under the name Juan David Gómez, who had been placed in state care after reportedly being brought to a hospital suffering from serious health problems. DNA samples from the child were compared with those of Rojas’ relatives.

Colombia’s attorney general said the results established that the boy was Rojas’ son.

Rojas was abducted in 2002 alongside presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt. She became pregnant and gave birth to Emmanuel while being held in the jungle. The child was later separated from her and eventually turned over to civilians, according to Colombian officials.

The finding supported Uribe’s claim that FARC did not have Emmanuel when it announced the planned release. The rebels had blamed Colombian military operations for preventing the handover, an accusation the government denied.

Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez had coordinated an international mission to receive the three hostages, sending aircraft and observers to Colombia. The operation was suspended when the rebels failed to provide a location for the exchange.

The DNA confirmation intensified criticism of FARC and raised new questions about Rojas’ condition and whereabouts. Emmanuel remained under government protection as officials considered arrangements for reuniting him with his maternal family.

Rojas and González remained in rebel captivity at the time, leaving the promised humanitarian release incomplete.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the 2007–2008 hostage drama involving FARC, Hugo Chavez, Clara Rojas, Consuelo Gonzalez, and the child known as Emmanuel, including the preliminary DNA findings.
counterfactuals.output:
The episode grew out of Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez’s attempt in 2007 to mediate a humanitarian exchange between Colombia and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC).

- **The hostages:**  
  - **Clara Rojas**, Ingrid Betancourt’s vice-presidential running mate, had been kidnapped with Betancourt in February 2002. While in captivity, Rojas became pregnant by a FARC member and gave birth around 2004 to a boy she named **Emmanuel**.  
  - **Consuelo González de Perdomo**, a former Colombian congresswoman, had been held since 2001.

- **Chávez’s role:** Colombian President Álvaro Uribe authorized Chávez to facilitate contacts with FARC in August 2007, but ended his formal mediation in November after Chávez communicated directly with Colombia’s army commander, contrary to Uribe’s instructions. FARC then announced that it would release Rojas, González, and Emmanuel to Chávez as a unilateral goodwill gesture.

- **“Operation Emmanuel”:** In late December 2007, Venezuelan helicopters, accompanied by international observers, flew into Colombia to receive the three. The handover repeatedly failed. FARC blamed Colombian military activity, but Uribe alleged that FARC could not produce Emmanuel because the child was no longer in its custody.

- **The child’s discovery and DNA evidence:** Colombian authorities identified a boy in state foster care, registered as **Juan David Gómez Tapiero**, who had been taken to a hospital in San José del Guaviare in 2005 suffering from serious illness, malnutrition, and injuries. Officials suspected he was Emmanuel. Preliminary Colombian DNA testing—using samples from the boy and members of Clara Rojas’s maternal family—found a very high probability that he belonged to the Rojas family. Mitochondrial DNA, which follows the maternal line, was reported as matching the maternal family profile; officials described the result as about **99.9 percent consistent with the relationship**, though independent confirmation was still being sought.

FARC then acknowledged that the boy in government care was Emmanuel, saying it had placed him with civilians because of his poor health. This admission largely vindicated Uribe’s claim that the group did not have all three promised captives when the original operation began.

On **January 10, 2008**, FARC finally released Clara Rojas and Consuelo González to a Venezuelan-led mission. Rojas was subsequently reunited with Emmanuel. The affair damaged FARC’s credibility while also highlighting Chávez’s controversial but, in this instance, partly successful role in securing hostage releases.
